name: Log jail
aka: the log gaol on the court-house square

documented_range.note: Andreas: 'During the fall of 1833, the citizens felt that something more metropolitan was required than the estray pen', and a log jail was built (docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 7, from Andreas I scan pp. 367 and 1243). A SEASON IS THE WHOLE OF THE DATING. 1833-10-01 is the middle of a northern-Illinois autumn and is a bound rather than a date; the building is standing well before the scene date on any reading of 'fall'. THE END IS A HOUSEKEEPING BOUND, NOT A DEMOLITION DATE - nothing reached says when this jail came down or was replaced, and 1835-12-31 is the ordinary continuity cut at the scene year this dataset uses where a fate is unattested.

change_note: The log jail the citizens put up on the north-west corner of the court-house square in the fall of 1833, because the estray pen at the other corner of the same block had until then been the town's only place of confinement. Standing on 1835-07-01. No change of fabric is attested inside the phase.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED AND THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED, so the tag follows the weaker half. Andreas puts the log jail on 'the northwest corner of the court-house square'. The public square is the block bounded by Randolph Street on the north, Washington Street on the south, Clark Street on the east and LaSalle Street on the west - the block this project's own ground control identifies as such in data/traces/gcp/wright_1834_gcps.json, where LaSalle and Randolph is labelled 'NW corner of the Public Square block' and Clark and Washington 'SE corner of the Public Square block'. Its four inside corners were computed for this parcel from modern OpenStreetMap intersection centres fetched 2026-08-11, offset 12.2 m into the block on each axis, half of an 80 ft street per Hathaway 1834: NW 447538.25 / 4637130.78, NE 447639.27 / 4637130.25, SW 447541.20 / 4637018.49, SE 447639.80 / 4637018.05, which makes the block about 101 x 112 m. The jail's own north-west corner is set on the square's north-west corner, so the footprint origin - which is the building's south-west corner - sits its own depth south of it. THIS IS A CORNER OF A BLOCK, NOT A LOT, so it is a weaker statement than the corner-lot placements elsewhere in this dataset: nothing says how far into the block the building stood, whether it was set back from either street line, or which way it faced. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference (data/datum.json: 17.5 m RMS on Wright 1834, 3.7 per cent paper stretch), plus an unquantified setback into the block. Facade bearing 0, due north onto Randolph, CONVENTION RATHER THAN EVIDENCE - a jail at the north-west corner could as reasonably have faced west onto LaSalle or inward onto the square, and nothing attests it. The square itself in 1835 was otherwise an open, unimproved prairie block, fenced or not; no fence, path or improvement of the block is modelled.
placement.symbolic_location: North-west corner of the court-house square (the public square bounded by Randolph, Clark, Washington and LaSalle), at the Randolph and LaSalle end; fronting north onto Randolph.

footprint.note: INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION, a plan, or a number of cells. 6.096 x 4.572 m is 20 x 15 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated per data/datum.json's units rule. The only constraint the evidence offers is relative and it runs in both directions: the jail was built because something more metropolitan was required than the estray pen, so it is a more substantial thing than a stock pound; and it was itself superseded within a few years, so it was small. A 20 x 15 ft log box is a two-cell lock-up and is the smallest thing that answers both. Nothing else about the shape is a finding: the plain rectangle, the proportion and the scale are all this record's.

construction.note: The building is named a LOG jail in the only description this project has of it, which makes the material the single best-attested thing about it. Hewn log with notched corners is what this archetype builds for that value; whether the walls were hewn or round, single or doubled, and whether they were lined, is unattested.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region, and it is what this project's other log buildings carry. The archetype would default a building this shallow to a shed roof, which is a covering appropriate to a lean-to; a purpose-built county jail is stated as gabled rather than left to that default. Typological derivation, not a measurement.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 32 degrees is this archetype's own default for a gable and is kept deliberately rather than replaced with a fresh guess - a new number would look like a finding and would not be one. It is lower than the 35-38 the dwelling archetypes use, which is the right direction: nobody framed a secondary building steeper than its covering required, and there is no loft under this roof.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.66 m is about 8 ft 9 in to the plate: a man's standing height with a header over the door and a course or two above it, which is what a lock-up needs and no more. It is also, to the centimetre, what this archetype's own size-aware default computes for a 20 x 15 ft footprint, and it is kept deliberately for the reason the roof pitch is. What is inferred is that the height falls in this range, not that it is exactly 2.66 m.

door.note: Not attested. `door` in this archetype names what has to get through the opening rather than whether there was one. A jail takes a person through in hand and nothing else - no horse, no wagon - so the man-door class is the reading, and it is the only one whose 1.88 m clear height fits under this wall. Where the door stood, what it was made of, and whether it was barred or grated is not attested and is the archetype's default.

function.note: Purpose-built for confinement, and it is the building that ended the practice recorded on the estray_pen record - prisoners held in the stock pound for want of anywhere else. Cook County was organised in 1831 and the county's business was conducted in rented rooms; this is the first purpose-built county structure of any kind and it precedes the court-house on the same block by about two years.

citations.citation: Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time. Vol. 1. Chicago: A. T. Andreas, 1884.
OpenStreetMap contributors. Street centerline intersection nodes for downtown Chicago, retrieved via the Overpass API, 2026-08-09.

research_note: A DOCUMENTED BUILDING WITH ONE DOCUMENTED ATTRIBUTE. What is attested is that it was a jail, that it was of logs, that it went up in the fall of 1833, and that it stood at the north-west corner of the court-house square. Everything else in this record - every dimension, the roof, the wall height, the door, the bearing - is inference or invention, and the confidence view will show it as such. THE RECORD IS WORTH HAVING ANYWAY, and this is the clearest case in the parcel for the working policy behind it: on 1835-07-01 the public square carried three things, a pound, a jail and (probably) a court-house, and a square rendered empty is a stronger and more misleading claim than a square carrying three honestly-graded conjectural boxes. ARCHETYPE CHOICE: outbuilding rather than log_dwelling, and the difference is not cosmetic. log_dwelling reads a storey count, a loft, a chimney count and a sign, and builds a dwelling's openings; outbuilding builds a plain box with one door sized by what has to get through it, and refuses a storey count outright. A jail is the second of those. The archetype's own family list - stable, shed, barn, smokehouse, privy, crib, woodshed - does not name a jail, and that is a gap in the vocabulary rather than a reason to build the wrong thing. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE THIS RECORD, in order of value: any county order or contract for the jail's construction, which is the kind of document that carries a dimension, a cost or a specification for the logs; Andreas vol. 1 at page-image level around scan pp. 367 and 1243, which is where the prose transcribed into this project's dossier sits; and the Cook County Sheriff's own published jail history, cited in the dossier and not yet held as a source record here.
